newsitem.title: INDIA: India housewife-turned-leader in first working day.
newsitem.headline: India housewife-turned-leader in first working day.

text.p: A housewife-turned-leader who was plucked out of her kitchen to rule India's second most populous state last week had her first regular day at work on Thursday, while her husband spent the day in jail.

Rabri Devi, a 38-year-old mother of nine children, was named as successor by former chief minister Laloo Prasad Yadav last Friday in the eastern Bihar state after a court issued a warrant for his arrest in a $280-million corruption scandal.

Devi, who has not studied beyond primary school, chaired a meeting of lawmakers, held a cabinet meeting, and met a horde of supporters under a mango tree at her residence on Thursday in the state capital, Patna.
Yadav, indicted by federal police, surrendered to a court on Wednesday and was remanded for two weeks.

"Even if she (Devi) is a housewife, she is a Durga (Hindu goddess). She will run an efficient government," said Brijesh Kumar, an activist of the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD), which rules the state of 93 million people, 61 percent of whom are illiterate.
The party has called for a general strike on Friday in support of the charismatic low-caste leader, who says he is innocent in the scandal involving alleged embezzlement of animal welfare funds.

After a weekend of political tumult in India springing from Yadav's choice, Devi won support from the state legislative assembly on Monday and formed on Tuesday a 75-member cabinet that critics said showed her desperation to woo political support.

She gained attention on Wednesday by dramatic events in which Yadav went in a motorcade to offer his arrest, a move opposition members and newspapers said was stage-managed to impress his command over millions of poor people in the state.

On Thursday, Devi, wearing a bright yellow sari and a violet Hindu vermillion mark on her forehead, received flowers and greetings from supporters who had come from all over the state to pledge their backing for the general strike.
"We said we have just come to say we are with you," said Abida Khatoon, an RJD leader.
Many women had colourful saris draped over their heads and veiled from the front to cover their faces. Some clutched children, and some touched her feet, while Devi said very little.
The gates of the colonial-style bungalow were open for all visitors, in contrast to the homes of most Indian leaders.
